intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hoxha-Aliu syndrome (HXAL) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ERI1 gene (608739) on chromosome 8p23.1.

checks.claim: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome (HXAL) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ERI1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we present a case of a female patient with a homozygous nonsense variant in ERI1 gene.
checks.explanation: The paper reports one homozygous nonsense ERI1 variant in an autosomal recessive syndrome. It does not use the name 'Hoxha-Aliu syndrome', and a single case does not establish the general claim that the syndrome is 'caused by' ERI1 mutation.

checks.evidence_quote: the patient presents with an 8p23.1 homozygous deletion, containing the microRNA miR-4660, the exoribonuclease 1 (ERI1), and malignant fibrous histiocytoma amplified sequence 1 (MFHAS1) genes

paragraphs.text: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are developmental delay or mild intellectual disability and distal limb abnormalities of the hands and feet (Hoxha and Aliu, 2023). Guo et al. (2023) found that individuals with biallelic null variants in ERI1 had mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies. They did not have the severe spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD) seen in individuals with biallelic ERI1 missense variants.

checks.claim: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: ERI1: A case report of an autosomal recessive syndrome associated with developmental delay and distal limb abnormalities.
checks.explanation: The title calls the syndrome autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: The main features of Hoxha-Aliu syndrome are developmental delay or mild intellectual disability and distal limb abnormalities of the hands and feet.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient exhibits mild intellectual disability, eyelid ptosis, and anomalies in her hands and feet
checks.explanation: Together with the title ('developmental delay and distal limb abnormalities'), this supports the stated main features.

checks.claim: Individuals with biallelic null variants in ERI1 had mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies.
checks.evidence_quote: but not in those with bi-allelic null variants, who showed mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies.

checks.claim: Individuals with biallelic null variants in ERI1 did not have the severe spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD) seen in individuals with biallelic ERI1 missense variants.
checks.evidence_quote: A severe spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD) was identified in five affected individuals with missense variants but not in those with bi-allelic null variants

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) described a girl (F5.II.1) with reduction defects of the hands and feet. On the right hand she had a transverse terminal limb reduction with a rudimentary fifth digit. Several digits had hypoplastic or absent nails. Toes 2 to 4 of the right foot and toes 3 to 5 of the left foot were absent, and there was syndactyly. She also had a perimembranous ventricular septal defect, pulmonary vein stenosis, microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. Her other features were brachycephaly with a flat occiput, bitemporal narrowing, a small nose, cupped prominent ears, and bilateral inguinal hernias. No vertebral or renal defects were recorded.

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) studied a girl (F5.II.1) with limb reduction defects, cardiac defects, microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. She carried a homozygous loss-of-function variant in the ERI1 gene (c.514C-T, Q172X). She was also homozygous for a missense variant in the KYNU gene (605197) (c.616G-A, E206K). The authors noted that ERI1 had previously been found, together with MFHAS1, in a homozygous microdeletion in a patient whose limb and cardiac abnormalities resembled hers. They suggested that the ERI1 variant may help explain her phenotype. However, they stated that the functional link between ERI1 mutation and these defects remained to be assessed.

paragraphs.text: Hoxha and Aliu (2023) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the ERI1 gene in a female patient with developmental delay and distal limb abnormalities. They described this as the first reported human case associated with ERI1 variants. They described ERI1 as an evolutionarily conserved 3-prime-to-5-prime exonuclease with an important function in multiple RNA processing pathways.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2023) identified biallelic null variants in the ERI1 gene in individuals with mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies. In 5 individuals with severe SEMD, they found biallelic missense variants instead. The missense variants abolished exoribonuclease activity. This caused defective trimming of the 3-prime end of 5.8S rRNA and reduced degradation of replication-dependent histone mRNAs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from affected individuals showed impaired chondrogenesis in vitro, with downregulation of genes that regulate skeletal patterning.
